transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, yeah, thank you for seeing me. I, um... well, I guess the main reason I’m here is that I’m just really struggling to get through my daily work. I teach high school, and obviously, that comes with a ton of grading and lesson planning. And I try, I really do try to stay on top of it. Like, I will set up my whole workspace at home—I'll get my coffee, make sure the room is quiet, clear off the desk, and I'll sit down with a big stack of student essays or some dense new curriculum document the district expects us to read through. 

I sit down fully intending to work, telling myself I'm going to just knock it out for the next hour. But then... I don't even know how it happens, but within ten minutes, I'll suddenly sort of snap back to reality and realize I’ve just been staring at the exact same page the entire time. I haven't actually processed a single word. Instead, I’m sitting there thinking about three completely unrelated things at once—like whether I need to get my car's oil changed, or replaying a weird interaction I had in the staff room, or just going down some random mental rabbit hole. I'm barely taking in what’s right in front of me, even though my eyes are literally on the paper. It’s just so exhausting because I end up wasting hours just trying to force myself to get through one single set of papers, and I just keep drifting off. It's really starting to pile up on me, so I figured I finally needed to come in and talk to somebody.
Have you noticed this kind of difficulty focusing and staying on task since you were a child or teenager, or is this something that started more recently?

Oh, no, it’s... yeah, it's definitely not a new thing at all. I mean, if I really sit down and think back on it, it’s been happening for pretty much as long as I can remember. Like, even way back in primary school, long before classes got dense or complicated, I was already having these exact same issues. 

I actually found a box of my old report cards a few years ago when I was helping my parents clear out their attic—which is a whole other story, because they've lived in that house for thirty years and absolutely refuse to throw anything away—but anyway, I was looking at these report cards from like, third and fourth grade. And almost every single one of my teachers wrote the exact same kind of comments in the little notes section at the bottom. They’d say things like, “He’s bright but careless,” or they'd write that I “doesn’t finish work unless closely supervised.” 

And looking back, it makes so much sense, because my parents were always getting so incredibly frustrated with me. They would go into my backpack to check for notes from the school, and they were constantly pulling out these completely crumpled, destroyed worksheets shoved all the way at the bottom of my bag. Like, I had actually done the work, or at least I had started it at my desk, but I just completely forgot to actually walk up and turn it in. My backpack was just this absolute black hole for paper. So yeah, I’d sit there at the kitchen table, and my mom would be hovering over me to make sure I finished my math, and the second she walked away to check on dinner or something, I’d be staring out the window at a bird and completely forget the worksheet existed. So, yes, it’s definitely been a lifelong pattern... it’s just that now, being the teacher myself, the stakes are so much higher and I don't have anyone looking over my shoulder to fish crumpled papers out of my bag, you know?

This is classic for predominantly inattentive ADHD.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with a lifelong, pervasive pattern of inattention—difficulty sustaining focus on tasks (grading, reading dense material), being easily distracted by internal thoughts, losing track of assignments, and failing to complete/turn in work—dating back to early elementary school (documented in old report cards with teacher comments such as 'bright but careless' and 'doesn't finish work unless closely supervised'). No reported history of hyperactivity or impulsivity, and no evidence of mood, anxiety, or psychotic symptoms accounting for the presentation. The chronicity, childhood onset, cross-situational nature (home and school), and current functional impairment (occupational difficulties as a teacher) support a diagnosis of ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation, rather than an anxiety disorder or unspecified ADHD.
